A late-night thought experiment

How I Ended Up Designing a Diamond Blob Space Program

It started with one innocent question — why isn't ion propulsion a thing? It ended, several hours later, with a shrink ray, a petawatt laser, a robot made of jelly, and a construction crew of a million blobs on Pluto. This is how we got there.

Published Saturday, November 21, 2026 Reading time about 7 minutes Regrets none

01 It started with a simple question

Why is ion propulsion not a thing? It sounds so easy. Zap some gas, shoot the ions out the back, off you go. Science fiction has been doing it for decades — surely reality is just being lazy?

Plot twist: ion propulsion is a thing. It's just a quiet, unglamorous thing that happens far away where nobody's watching. NASA's Dawn spacecraft cruised the asteroid belt on ion thrusters, visiting Vesta and Ceres. BepiColombo is riding ion engines to Mercury as you read this. The technology works beautifully.

The catch is thrust. An ion engine pushes with roughly the force of a sheet of paper resting on your hand — millinewtons. It can run for months, so in the vacuum of space that whisper of a push adds up to real speed. But it will never, ever lift anything off Earth. And the "easy" part is deceptive: stripping electrons off xenon atoms and accelerating the ions through high-voltage grids that slowly erode, powered by solar arrays or a reactor, in hard vacuum only — that's the actual engineering. Simple idea, fussy machine.

~90 mN
Dawn's ion thrust — about the weight of a sheet of paper
30–50 km/s
Ion exhaust speed, vs ~4.5 km/s for a chemical rocket
6–7 m/s
Extra speed Dawn gained per day of continuous thrust

02 Fine. Take it to Pluto

Every good rabbit hole has a moment where someone says "okay, but what about Pluto?" This was that moment.

Does sunlight even reach that far? Yes — barely. Pluto sits about 40 times farther from the Sun than Earth, and light dims with the square of the distance, so Pluto gets roughly 1/1600th of our sunlight. Twilight-level. Enough to read by, nowhere near enough to run a serious solar-powered spaceship.

Which is why real missions out there go nuclear. New Horizons, which flew past Pluto in 2015, ran on an RTG — essentially a chunk of plutonium whose heat becomes electricity. Bolt that power source to an ion engine and the Pluto trip works in principle. There's no top speed in space; there's only how fast you accumulate it. Dawn gained about 6–7 meters per second per day. Over years of patient thrusting, a nuclear ion ship could eventually outrun Voyager 1 — still the fastest thing we've ever launched at about 17 km/s, and it got there the loud way, with chemical rockets and gravity assists stolen from Jupiter and Saturn.

Ion is a marathon, not a sprint. Which raises the obvious question…

03 A Ladder of Propulsion Ideas

Four ways to go faster, ranked from "actually flown" to "catching a laser and riding it like a rail."

  1. Chemical rockets + gravity assists

    17 km/s — Voyager 1

    Still the fastest thing ever flown. Chemical exhaust tops out around 4–5 km/s, so the real trick is stealing speed from planets as you swing past them.

  2. Nuclear thermal

    ~2× chemical efficiency

    Run hydrogen through a reactor core and blast it out the back: roughly double a chemical rocket's efficiency, but with real, honest thrust. NASA and DARPA pursued this as DRACO. And since it's still a ship flying past planets, it can steal gravity assists from Jupiter just like a chemical rocket — try it in the playground.

  3. Project Orion

    a few % of light speed

    The 1960s plan to propel a ship by detonating small nuclear bombs behind a giant steel pusher plate and riding the shockwaves. Absurd on paper, sound in the math, killed by the test ban treaty and common sense. Even a ship this absurd can still swing past Jupiter for a free gravity assist on the way out — try it in the playground. Also — and this is the risk nobody put in the official report — keep hammering space with nuclear blasts and you have to wonder what you're rattling loose. The Phantom Zone is not famous for its sturdy locks, and a steady drumbeat of explosions feels like exactly the kind of thing that cracks the door just wide enough for General Zod to slip out, take one look at your ship, and tell everyone aboard to kneel. Hard to pitch mission control on a propulsion system whose worst-case failure mode is a Kryptonian warlord with a grudge.

  4. Laser sail

    20% of light speed — the plan

    No fuel at all: a giant laser array pushes a tiny sail with light itself. Breakthrough Starshot wants to send a gram-sized chip to another star this way, within a human lifetime. One trick it can't use: gravity assist — at up to 20% of light speed, a planet's few km/s of help is a rounding error, and the beam fixes the sail's path anyway.

How the real Starshot burn works: the sail gets essentially all of its speed in the first few minutes, while it is still within about 0.12 AU of Earth and the beam is still tight — then the laser switches off and it coasts at 60,000 km/s. There is no push left to fade out at Pluto. And why no gravity-assist button? At 60,000 km/s, Jupiter could add only a few km/s — a rounding error — and the beam from Earth locks the sail to a straight line, so it can't steer into a precise planetary flyby anyway. Gravity assist is for ships that can aim; the sail just rides the light.

Pick an engine and punch it. Voyager 1 — the speed to beat — cruises at 17 km/s. Planet positions are square-root compressed so the inner planets aren't invisible; Pluto really is 39.5 AU out. Physics: napkin-grade, as is tradition.

04 The laser rail

Somewhere in the laser-sail discussion, a better metaphor showed up: not a sail being shoved by light, but a particle riding in a light field — a laser rail. And here's the delightful part: that's not far from real physics. In laboratories, optical tweezers use focused laser beams to trap and guide microscopic particles exactly like beads sliding along a rail.

The catch, as always, is scale. Light spreads. A laser beam diffracts and widens over distance, so the rail gets fatter and weaker the farther you ride it — unless you install relay lenses along the way, or use exotic beam shapes like Bessel beams that barely spread at all. But the core intuition holds: shape light into a track, and the ship rides the field instead of being pushed by it.

Optical tweezers, however, work on things the size of bacteria. For the laser rail to work as-is, the ship has to be bacteria-adjacent. Which means there's really only one solution.

“So, for it to work as is, I need to figure out Honey, I Shrunk the Kids.”

— The exact moment this stopped being a physics question

05 Honey, I shrunk the spaceship

Bad news first: you cannot shrink a person. A human is roughly 1028 atoms, atoms are a fixed size, and the Bohr radius does not negotiate. There is no ray.

Good news: scientists have shrunk objects — just not originals. In 2018, MIT published implosion fabrication: 3D-print a structure inside a hydrogel, then dehydrate it so the whole thing shrinks to about a tenth of its size, down to the nanoscale. It's a high-tech Shrinky Dink, and it's genuinely useful for tiny lenses and medical devices.

So the real-world shrink ray is: don't shrink the thing — build a tiny copy of the thing. Which is, not coincidentally, exactly what Breakthrough Starshot already proposes. The shrink ray is optional. Making the ship absurdly tiny is the actual plan.

06 Or: wrap a person in diamond

The alternative — scale the sail up to the person instead of shrinking the person down to the sail — deserves its moment, because the math is gloriously brutal.

Sunlight pushes with about 9 micronewtons per square meter. A sail a full kilometer across, in direct sunlight, gets about 9 newtons of push — roughly the weight of a bag of sugar. To accelerate one person at a gentle 0.1g, you'd need a sail of 10+ square kilometers, before adding the ship, the food, and the air. Sunlight alone won't do it; you need the laser. Starshot's plan uses about 100 gigawatts to push a one-gram chip. Scale that to a 100-kilo person and you're at roughly ten petawatts — thousands of times everything humanity generates.

Hence: wrap the person in diamond. It's a sneaky-good material pick. Diamond conducts heat about five times better than copper, and it's transparent to many laser wavelengths, so a diamond sail lets the beam pass through instead of soaking it up and melting — diamond films are genuinely on the list of proposed lightsail materials. And the petawatts? Possible, in principle, with a concentrated fusion reaction — a mere million times what ITER is designed to produce. At some point in this design process, "just build a petawatt fusion plant" stopped sounding like the craziest item on the list.

But we don't actually need the person. We need the person's eyes. And eyes can be much, much smaller.

07 Enter the blob

The design that emerged, in full: a robot built in a blobby liquid that shrinks like a Shrinky Dink. The liquid is piezoelectric, so it forms the circuitry as it flexes. It carries sensors and compute. Seal it inside a tiny diamond — transparent, so it can see out; tough, so it can take the beam — and you have eyes that can travel across the solar system.

Honestly? As a concept, it holds together better than it has any right to. The diamond is the hull. The hydrogel body is the MIT shrink trick. Piezoelectric gel gives you circuits that bend instead of snapping; liquid-metal traces could wire the rest. The remaining problems are the honest kind: power, and phoning home across billions of kilometers with a laser link aimed with absurd precision. But the ship itself? The ship is a gemstone with a jelly robot inside, and I would fund that Kickstarter.

08 Meanwhile, on Pluto: the power problem

Two challenges remain, and they're the real ones. First: build a laser on Pluto — solved, elegantly, by sending blob robots one at a time that assemble and disassemble, a self-building construction crew. Second: power it. Every option has a catch.

Ruled out

Solar panels on Pluto

Under 1 watt per square meter out there. Powering even a megawatt laser would take a solar farm the size of a city. Scratch that.

The favorite

Ship a fission reactor, in pieces

Blob-sized reactor modules, assembled on arrival. A few kilos of uranium fuel runs for years — the shipping cost is the hardware, not the fuel. NASA's Kilopower design is the template.

Rejected — safety

Beam the power from near the Sun

Collect sunlight where it's strong and laser it to Pluto. Elegant — until a rotating planet drifts into a petawatt beam and gets carved by it. A power beam and a death ray are the same device, pointed differently. Hard pass.

Someday, maybe

Mine Pluto for fusion fuel

Pluto has water ice; water has deuterium. In principle, local fusion fuel. In practice, it requires a working fusion reactor — a harder problem than the laser.

The verdict, for now: power is an open question, and that's okay. Every source has a catch — solar is too weak, fission means shipping a mountain one blob at a time, beamed power risks sweeping a planet, and fusion is fusion. The rest of the design holds up. Power is the one box still marked figure this out later.

09 How many blobs does a reactor take?

Time for a Fermi estimate — the kind of math you do on a napkin, which is the correct napkin for this entire project. Say each blob is 10 grams: chunkier than Starshot's gram-scale chip, because ours carries tools. A 1-megawatt reactor, scaled from Kilopower, masses roughly 10 tonnes. Ten tonnes is ten million grams. You can see where this is going.

≈ 10 tonnes of reactor, shipped 10 grams at a time. A million-blob job — almost feasible, if you're launching them by the thousand.

And it scales brutally. A gigawatt laser needs a billion blobs. A petawatt laser needs a trillion, and at that point you're shipping more mass than a small mountain to Pluto, ten grams at a time. The blob count is set by the laser's appetite.

10 One laser, many blobs: the pipeline

One more idea, and it's a good one: can you pipeline the blobs on the same ray — fire them one after another on the same energy output? Yes. That's exactly how Starshot is meant to work: you don't retire the laser after one probe. It launches them in sequence, each getting its turn on the beam.

The catch is that energy is a budget, and it splits. Every blob needs a fixed amount of kinetic energy to reach a given speed, so a million blobs at full speed cost a million times the energy of one. Same laser, same total output: each blob goes slower, or you wait longer between launches while the capacitors recharge. And they can't share the beam simultaneously — the lead sail blocks the light for everyone behind it, like a convoy where only the first truck gets the sun. Launch one, let it get far ahead, slew the beam, launch the next. Pipelining works. Throughput is limited by total energy, not by how many blobs you can line up.

Notice the pattern? It's the same pattern as everything else tonight.

Every rabbit hole, accounted for

  • Ion propulsion (Dawn, BepiColombo, paper-weight thrust)
  • Sunlight at Pluto: 1/1600th, twilight-level
  • RTGs and New Horizons' plutonium battery
  • Voyager 1 at 17 km/s, the speed to beat
  • Nuclear thermal and the DRACO program
  • Project Orion: propulsion by nuclear bomb
  • Breakthrough Starshot's gram-sized chip
  • The laser rail and optical tweezers
  • Bessel beams that barely spread
  • The shrink ray that doesn't exist (Bohr radius)
  • MIT implosion fabrication — high-tech Shrinky Dinks
  • A kilometer of sail = one bag of sugar of push
  • Ten petawatts to launch one (1) person
  • Wrapping the person in diamond
  • Petawatt fusion, a million ITERs
  • The piezoelectric blob robot, sealed in diamond
  • Self-assembling blob crews on Pluto
  • Kilopower reactors, shipped in pieces
  • Beamed power, rejected: planets might get blasted
  • Fusion fuel mined from Pluto's ice
  • One million blobs per megawatt (Fermi-certified)
  • Pipelining blobs on a single laser
  • Patent? White paper? Blog won — publishing is prior art

Energy is the limiting factor. It always was.

If there's one thing this whole exercise taught me, it's that. Every idea we bounced around — ion, chemical, nuclear thermal, laser sails, riding bombs, riding light — is really just a different answer to the same question: how much energy can you bring, and how efficiently can you turn it into speed?

The physics of moving through space is easy. The physics of carrying enough energy to do it fast is the whole game. Whoever cracks cheap, dense, abundant energy doesn't just unlock the solar system. They unlock everything after it.

Until then: the blobs are ready when the power is.

Written from a real late-night conversation that began with “Why is ion propulsion not a thing?” — every idea above was genuinely explored along the way, including the ones we rejected. Numbers are the conversation's own back-of-the-napkin figures; treat the trillion-blob estimates accordingly. Illustrations are artist's impressions — the real blob, when it exists, will presumably be even cuter.
